title: UPGRADING the Letter Grading System in Middle and High School
author: Nick Potkalitsky
summary: Terry Underwood, introduced by Potkalitsky, surveys how external standardized testing and internal letter grading coexist in American high schools with opposing purposes. He traces the industrial model of schooling and the sociological forces that keep it in place, and argues that tests privilege psychometric precision while grades, though unreliable singly, aggregate into a robust GPA. He reviews evidence that grades damage motivation and that test pressure erodes teachers' knowledge of their students. He then sorts current reform efforts into four themes: alternative grading, equity and mental health, technology, and context. His conclusion is that individual teachers tinkering alone will not change the system, and that local collaborative assessment among department colleagues is the lever for grades that reflect real learning.
points: External tests and internal grades serve different purposes, yet policy privileges the former because their psychometric properties are better studied, which shapes pedagogy.
GPA aggregated across many teachers is more reliable than any single grade and may be worth keeping, even as the research on grades' harm to motivation says practice must change.
Test pressure and alignment to external standards can pull teachers into scripted, prealigned instruction and displace their knowledge of individual learners.
Grade reformers cluster in four themes: alternative grading, equity and mental health, technology and data, and grading in context.
Solitary tinkering yields scattered enlightened classrooms; durable change needs teachers to build assessment together at the department level.
quotes: Grades can increase fear of failure, reduce interest and creativity, increase anxiety, and lead struggling students to withdraw. High-achieving students may be motivated to keep getting good grades, but this effort doesn't translate into deep and intentional learning. Grades don't communicate what students have actually learned, just points earned.

Letter grades are notoriously unreliable in isolation. It’s hard to know what factors individual teachers consider, and they can change. For example, some teachers reward effort, attendance, and growth. Others reward individual accomplishment on what they consider objective exams. But when ten or twenty or thirty grades are given to one student over several years with different teachers, reliability gets better and better.

Literacy research (Johnston, Afflerbach, and Weiss, 1993, Educational Assessment) has shown troubling effects in schools where there is intense pressure to raise test scores. Teachers actually knew less about their students' individual reading and writing attitudes and experiences in schools under “heavy threat” from test machinery compared to teachers in schools with less pressure, one large-scale study of two large districts revealed.

Standardized test scores correlate well with socioeconomic status of the school population. Historically, remediation of deficiencies in a high-poverty school because of low scores brings about draconian pedagogical mandates like required materials and assignments and scripted teaching.

Grades constructed from rigid rubrics and viewed alongside normative test scores would decontextualize human aspects of learning to provide interval data , which can be added, subtracted, multiplied, divided—portable data which can fit in a cell of a spreadsheet—and converted to standard scores. In this system we would have successfully disappeared the learner.

Tinkering with traditional grading systems by individual teachers, working alone under the expectation that piecemeal adjustments will lead to substantive change, is not likely to have much impact. I liken this approach to "a thousand flowers blooming” because while it may result in random enlightened classrooms across schools, it fails to address the inherent flaws and systemic negative impact of grading on learning.

Grades have been repeatedly shown to inadequately measure actual learning, to diminish genuine engagement, to poorly motivate sustained learning, to encourage competition over collaboration, to provide insufficient feedback for growth, to perpetuate inequities, and to suffer from subjectivity and inconsistency. These are not isolated failings but rather predictable outcomes of a flawed system.
